title: Non-compete clauses in employment contracts
reasons: labour -2: Restraints keep a large share of the workforce from moving to rivals. | entry-exit -1: Workers cannot leave to start competing firms.
summary: Non-compete clauses bind about one in five workers. They keep people from moving to better-paid jobs with rivals or starting their own firms: one of the clearest barriers to labour mobility in Australia.

title: Gatekeeper digital platforms
reasons: competition -1: Gatekeeper platforms face little competition in app distribution, search and ad tech. | innovation -1: Platform rules and self-preferencing can disadvantage rival apps and services.
summary: A handful of platforms control app stores, search and digital advertising. Businesses that depend on them face the platforms' terms and self-preferencing, which can blunt competition and new services.

title: Domestic airline duopoly
reasons: competition -2: Two groups carry about 98% of domestic passengers. | entry-exit -1: Airport slots, aircraft and scale make entry hard; two entrants failed in 2024.
summary: Two airline groups carry almost all domestic passengers, after two challengers failed in 2024. Fares face little competitive pressure, and new entrants struggle to get slots and scale.

title: Higher prices for customers who do not switch
reasons: competition -1: Customers who do not switch pay more, so firms face less pressure to compete on price.
summary: Firms charge loyal customers more than new ones in several essential services. Weak switching dulls price competition; the default electricity offers in the register were a response.

title: Market power of the major banks
reasons: competition -2: The major banks have sustained prices above competitive levels (Productivity Commission, 2018). | entry-exit -1: Funding cost advantages from size, credit ratings and internal risk models make it harder for smaller lenders to grow.
summary: The four major banks have market power the Productivity Commission called a defining feature of the financial system. Banking is an input to every industry, so weak competition there raises costs across the economy.

title: Slow recognition of overseas-trained health practitioners
reasons: labour -1: Slow, costly recognition narrows the pool of practitioners who can work in Australia.
summary: Overseas-trained health practitioners wait a long time, and pay a lot, to be recognised, with specialist colleges assessing their peers. It holds back supply in one of the largest workforces.

title: Concentrated supermarket market
reasons: competition -2: An oligopoly of two chains faces limited pressure to compete on price. | entry-exit -1: The incumbents' scale and store networks make entry and expansion costly for rivals.
summary: Two chains dominate grocery retailing, and the ACCC found them among the most profitable supermarkets in the world relative to peers. Weak rivalry in the biggest consumer market keeps prices and margins high.

title: Automatic mutual recognition of occupational registrations (ACT)
reasons: labour +1: Removes the application and fee a licensed worker needed before working across the border. | market-integration +1: Recognises other participating jurisdictions' registrations, moving towards one national market for licensed services.
summary: Lets tradespeople, real estate agents and other licensed workers registered in one participating state work in another without applying or paying again. A modest gain for labour mobility and for a national market in licensed services; there is little evidence yet on its size.

title: Design and Building Practitioners Act registration scheme (NSW)
reasons: burden -1: Adds registration, design compliance declarations and documentation for every class 2 (apartment) project. | labour -1: Only registered practitioners may design or certify apartment work, narrowing who can supply it.
summary: Requires designers, builders and engineers on apartment projects to register and to declare that designs and work comply. It aims to cut building defects; the productivity cost is the paperwork and the narrower pool of practitioners who may do the work.

title: Professional engineers registration scheme (Victoria)
reasons: labour -1: Only registered engineers may provide services in prescribed areas, narrowing the pool of suppliers. | burden -1: Adds registration, assessment and continuing development requirements for engineering firms.
summary: Requires professional engineers in prescribed areas to register. It aims to protect building users; the productivity cost is a new condition on who can supply engineering services, and the cost of registration.

title: Surcharges removed on eftpos, Mastercard and Visa; lower interchange caps
reasons: competition +1: The headline price is the price paid, so prices are easier to compare. | prices-taxes -1: Card acceptance costs are spread across all customers, weakening the signal to use cheaper payment methods; lower interchange caps cut the cost itself.
summary: Bans surcharges on eftpos, Mastercard and Visa cards and lowers interchange caps. The price shown is the price paid, and acceptance costs fall; but card costs are now spread across all customers rather than charged to card users.

title: Card surcharges limited to the cost of acceptance
reasons: prices-taxes +1: Surcharges must reflect the cost of card acceptance. | competition +1: Stops excessive surcharges being used as a hidden margin, making prices easier to compare.
summary: Card surcharges may not exceed what accepting the card costs the merchant. Prices become clearer and surcharges can no longer be a hidden margin.

title: National Quality Framework for early childhood education and care (all jurisdictions except WA)
reasons: burden -1: Adds assessment and rating, documentation and quality improvement planning for every service. | entry-exit -1: Higher staff ratios and qualification requirements raise the cost of opening a centre, weighing most on small providers. | competition +1: Published quality ratings give parents information to compare services. | market-integration +1: One national framework replaced separate state and territory licensing regimes.
summary: One national law for childcare quality: national standards, ratings, staff ratios and qualifications replaced separate state rules. Quality ratings help parents compare centres, but ratio and qualification rules raise the cost of opening and running a centre.

title: National Quality Framework commences in Western Australia
reasons: burden -1: Adds assessment and rating, documentation and quality improvement planning for every service. | entry-exit -1: Higher staff ratios and qualification requirements raise the cost of opening a centre, weighing most on small providers. | competition +1: Published quality ratings give parents information to compare services. | market-integration +1: One national framework replaced separate state and territory licensing regimes.
summary: One national law for childcare quality: national standards, ratings, staff ratios and qualifications replaced separate state rules. Quality ratings help parents compare centres, but ratio and qualification rules raise the cost of opening and running a centre. Western Australia joined seven months after the other jurisdictions.

title: Fee growth cap for services taking the early childhood worker retention payment
reasons: prices-taxes -1: A cap on fee growth ties prices to a set rate rather than to each service's costs. | capital -1: Capped revenue growth lowers the expected return on new or expanded centres. | labour +1: The payment funds a wage rise that helps attract and keep qualified educators.
summary: Services taking the worker retention payment must hold fee growth to about 4.4% a year. It funds higher pay for educators but caps prices for services whose costs rise faster, which may slow expansion.

title: Conveyance duty abolished on commercial property up to $1.5 million (ACT)
reasons: prices-taxes +2: Removes or replaces a transaction tax that Treasury estimates costs 72 cents of efficiency per extra dollar raised. | capital +1: Lowers the up-front cost of buying business premises.
summary: The ACT abolished conveyance duty on commercial property up to $1.5 million, moving to annual rates. Stamp duty is one of the most inefficient taxes: it discourages firms from moving to better premises and makes property slower to change hands.

title: Stamp duty on non-residential property phased out (South Australia)
reasons: prices-taxes +2: Removes or replaces a transaction tax that Treasury estimates costs 72 cents of efficiency per extra dollar raised. | capital +1: Lowers the up-front cost of buying business premises.
summary: South Australia abolished stamp duty on commercial and industrial property transfers in three steps to 2018. Stamp duty is one of the most inefficient taxes: it discourages firms from moving to better premises and makes property slower to change hands.

title: Commercial and industrial property tax replaces stamp duty (Victoria)
reasons: prices-taxes +2: Removes or replaces a transaction tax that Treasury estimates costs 72 cents of efficiency per extra dollar raised. | capital +1: Lowers the up-front cost of buying business premises.
summary: Victoria replaces stamp duty on commercial and industrial property with an annual property tax, one property at a time from its next sale; the full effect builds over decades. Stamp duty is one of the most inefficient taxes: it discourages firms from moving to better premises and makes property slower to change hands.

title: National small amount credit contract regime and cost caps
reasons: market-integration +1: One national regime replaced differing state caps. | prices-taxes -1: Binding caps on fees can ration credit to borrowers whose risk costs more to serve. | entry-exit -1: Lower allowed margins push some small lenders out.
summary: A national regime with caps on the cost of small loans replaced differing state caps. The caps protect borrowers but can push smaller lenders out and ration credit to riskier borrowers.

title: Consumer Data Right: open banking
reasons: competition +1: Portable account data lower search and switching costs. | innovation +1: Data access lets new firms build comparison and other services. | burden -1: Banks bear substantial build and compliance costs for the data-sharing system.
summary: Banks must share customers' data, with consent, with accredited providers. Portable data should make it easier to compare and switch, and lets new services be built; take-up has been slow and compliance costs high.

title: Container deposit scheme (ACT)
reasons: burden -1: Suppliers must register every container type and report and pay scheme costs. | market-integration -1: Each state's scheme has its own registration and cost recovery, adding costs to selling in several states. | prices-taxes +1: The deposit puts a price on littered and landfilled containers, a cost the market otherwise ignores.
summary: Beverage suppliers fund a 10-cent refund on containers. It prices litter and waste more fully, but each state runs its own scheme, with its own registration and costs, which weighs most on small and interstate suppliers.

title: New motor accident injuries (CTP) scheme (ACT)
reasons: burden +1: Defined benefits reduce the legal and claims-handling costs of fault-based disputes.
summary: Replaced the ACT's fault-based compulsory third-party scheme with defined benefits. Fewer disputes over fault cut the legal and claims costs of the scheme; insurers already competed, so the competition effect is small.

title: New compulsory third-party (green slip) scheme (New South Wales)
reasons: burden +1: Defined benefits reduce the legal and claims-handling costs of fault-based disputes. | competition -1: Profit normalisation and risk equalisation narrow the room for insurers to compete on price.
summary: A new compulsory third-party scheme with defined benefits for most injuries, insurer profit normalisation and risk equalisation. Claims costs and premiums fell, but limits on profits and risk pricing narrow how insurers compete.

title: Compulsory third-party insurance opened to private insurers and price competition (South Australia)
reasons: competition +2: Moves from a single insurer and then a common price to price competition among four insurers. | entry-exit +1: Opened compulsory third-party insurance to licensed private insurers.
summary: South Australia replaced its single public insurer with four private insurers (2016) and then let them compete on price (2019).

title: Default Market Offer price cap (NSW, SEQ, SA)
reasons: prices-taxes -1: A regulated default price replaces retailer-set standing offers and may sit away from some retailers' costs. | competition +1: A common reference price makes offers easier to compare and curbs the 'loyalty tax' on customers who do not switch. | entry-exit -1: Lower standing-offer margins can deter smaller retailers from entering or expanding.
summary: Caps standing-offer electricity prices in New South Wales, south-east Queensland and South Australia, and makes retailers quote discounts against the same reference price. It protects customers who do not shop around, but a regulated price can compress the margins entrants rely on.

title: Victorian Default Offer
reasons: prices-taxes -1: A regulated default price replaces retailer-set standing offers and may sit away from some retailers' costs. | competition +1: A common reference price makes offers easier to compare and curbs the 'loyalty tax' on customers who do not switch. | entry-exit -1: Lower standing-offer margins can deter smaller retailers from entering or expanding.
summary: Victoria's regulator sets a default electricity price for customers who do not choose a market offer, and retailers must tell customers about their best offer. It protects customers who do not shop around, but a regulated price can compress the margins entrants rely on.

title: Mandatory electronic conveyancing (New South Wales)
reasons: burden +1: Electronic lodgement and settlement cut paperwork, settlement time and errors. | innovation +1: Moves conveyancing onto a digital platform. | competition -1: Without interoperability, mandatory electronic lodgement entrenched one network (PEXA) as a near-monopoly supplier.
summary: Requires property transfers and mortgages to be lodged electronically. Settlement is faster and cheaper, but with no working interoperability between networks the mandate entrenched a single lodgement network.

title: East-coast gas price cap and Gas Market Code
reasons: prices-taxes -2: A binding price control in a major input market keeps prices from signalling scarcity. | capital -1: Price controls and exemptions negotiated case by case add regulatory risk to gas supply investment.
summary: An emergency cap on east-coast wholesale gas prices, then a mandatory code with a 'reasonable price' rule. It lowered input costs for gas users, but controls on the price of a major input dull the signal for new supply and add regulatory risk for investors.

title: Full retail contestability for electricity (Queensland)
reasons: entry-exit +2: Removes the incumbent's exclusive right to small customers, opening the market to new retailers. | competition +1: Customers can switch retailer, so retailers must compete for them.
summary: Ended the incumbent retailer's exclusive right to supply small electricity customers, so every customer could choose a retailer.

title: Full retail contestability for small electricity customers (Tasmania)
reasons: entry-exit +2: Removes the incumbent's exclusive right to small customers, opening the market to new retailers. | competition +1: Customers can switch retailer, so retailers must compete for them.
summary: Ended the incumbent retailer's exclusive right to supply small electricity customers, so every customer could choose a retailer. In Tasmania few retailers entered, because the market is small and prices stayed regulated.

title: Multi-employer bargaining streams
reasons: labour -1: Common terms across employers reduce firms' flexibility to match pay and job design to their own productivity. | competition -1: Competing employers bargaining together on labour costs dampens rivalry between them.
summary: New bargaining streams let one agreement cover several employers. It may lift pay in low-paid care sectors but sets common terms across competing employers and reduces firms' flexibility to organise work.

title: Right to disconnect
reasons: burden -1: Employers need policies and practices to manage out-of-hours contact and disputes.
summary: Employees may refuse unreasonable contact outside working hours. A workplace right aimed at wellbeing; for firms it adds policies and some coordination costs.

title: Same Job Same Pay orders for labour hire
reasons: labour -1: Reduces the flexibility of labour hire as a way to add workers quickly. | burden -1: Orders, exemptions and pay comparisons add compliance costs for hosts and providers.
summary: The Fair Work Commission can order labour-hire firms to pay at least the host's enterprise agreement rates. It raises the cost and reduces the flexibility of labour hire, a way firms scale their workforce.

title: Next-day fuel price commitment, MyFuel NT (Northern Territory)
reasons: competition -1: Limits when retailers can change prices, and advance commitments make rivals' prices easy to match. | burden -1: Retailers must set and report the next day's price within a daily window.
summary: Retailers must post tomorrow's price the day before and may only cut it during the day, as in Perth. It ends sudden price jumps, but restricting price changes and publishing commitments in advance can make prices easier to match; Perth's experience does not show a clear fall in average margins.

title: Daily fuel price cap: next-day maximum price (Victoria)
reasons: competition -1: Limits when retailers can change prices, and advance commitments make rivals' prices easy to match. | burden -1: Retailers must set and report the next day's price within a daily window.
summary: Retailers must post tomorrow's price the day before and may only cut it during the day, as in Perth. It ends sudden price jumps, but restricting price changes and publishing commitments in advance can make prices easier to match; Perth's experience does not show a clear fall in average margins.

title: Mandatory fuel price reporting, FuelCheck (New South Wales)
reasons: competition +1: Real-time public prices cut motorists' search costs; the risk that rivals use them to coordinate tempers the gain. | burden -1: Retailers must register sites and report each price change within a set time.
summary: Retailers must report every price change for publication, so motorists can find the cheapest fuel. Lower search costs should sharpen price competition, but rivals also see each other's prices at once, which can help them coordinate.

title: Future Gaming Market: end of the Federal Group gaming monopoly (Tasmania)
reasons: competition +1: Removes the upstream monopoly over gaming machine operation in venues.
summary: Hotels and clubs hold gaming machine licences directly, ending one company's monopoly on machines outside casinos. A cap on machine numbers remains.

title: Venue-operator model for gaming machines; end of the Tatts-Tabcorp duopoly (Victoria)
reasons: competition +1: Removes the upstream duopoly, letting venues operate machines directly.
summary: Pubs and clubs own or lease gaming machines under ten-year entitlements, replacing the Tatts and Tabcorp duopoly. Entitlement auctions and caps may concentrate venue ownership.

title: Concerted practices prohibition and other Harper CCA reforms
reasons: competition +1: Lets regulators act against coordination between rivals that falls short of a contract.
summary: Competition law now prohibits concerted practices that substantially lessen competition, reaching coordination short of an agreement. Stronger enforcement against tacit collusion across the economy.

title: Misuse of market power: effects test (s 46)
reasons: competition +1: Makes conduct by dominant firms that harms competition easier to challenge. | entry-exit +1: Lowers the risk that dominant firms block rivals' entry or growth.
summary: An 'effects test' for misuse of market power: a firm with substantial market power may not act with the purpose or effect of substantially lessening competition. It makes exclusionary conduct by dominant firms easier to challenge.

title: National registration of health practitioners (the ACT)
reasons: labour +2: Removes the need to re-register when moving between states, for hundreds of thousands of practitioners. | market-integration +1: One national scheme and standards replaced separate state and territory boards.
summary: One national registration for health practitioners replaced separate state boards, so a registered nurse, doctor or other practitioner can work in any state. A large gain for mobility in one of the biggest workforces.

title: Heavy Vehicle National Law commences (ACT)
reasons: market-integration +1: A single national law and regulator replaced state-by-state rules for heavy vehicles. | burden +1: Interstate operators deal with one set of rules and one regulator instead of several.
summary: One national heavy vehicle law and regulator replaced differing state rules on fatigue, mass, dimensions and access. It lowers compliance costs for interstate freight operators, though the law has been criticised as complex and access permits were slow at first.

reasons: market-integration +1: A single national law and regulator replaced state-by-state rules for heavy vehicles. | burden +1: Interstate operators deal with one set of rules and one regulator instead of several.
summary: One national heavy vehicle law and regulator replaced differing state rules on fatigue, mass, dimensions and access. It lowers compliance costs for interstate freight operators, though the law has been criticised as complex and access permits were slow at first.

title: Mandatory Dairy Code of Conduct
reasons: competition +1: Constrains the conduct of the stronger party in the supply chain, countering bargaining power. | burden -1: Adds contracting, disclosure and dispute-resolution requirements.
summary: A mandatory code for milk supply agreements between dairy farmers and processors, with published minimum prices and limits on retrospective price cuts. It counters processors' bargaining power but limits contracting flexibility.

title: Mandatory Food and Grocery Code of Conduct
reasons: competition +1: Constrains the conduct of the stronger party in the supply chain, countering bargaining power. | burden -1: Adds contracting, disclosure and dispute-resolution requirements.
summary: A mandatory Food and Grocery Code with civil penalties governs how large supermarkets and wholesalers deal with suppliers. It counters the buying power of a concentrated retail sector, at a compliance cost.

title: Remade Franchising Code of Conduct
reasons: competition +1: Constrains the conduct of the stronger party in the supply chain, countering bargaining power. | burden -1: Adds contracting, disclosure and dispute-resolution requirements.
summary: The remade Franchising Code strengthens disclosure and franchisee protections. Better-informed franchisees can compete on fairer terms, but compliance costs can deter new franchise systems.

title: New mandatory Horticulture Code of Conduct
reasons: competition +1: Constrains the conduct of the stronger party in the supply chain, countering bargaining power. | burden -1: Adds contracting, disclosure and dispute-resolution requirements.
summary: A mandatory code requiring written agreements and price transparency between growers and traders. It strengthens growers' bargaining position, with compliance costs for traders.

title: Sugar Industry Code of Conduct
reasons: competition +1: Growers may choose their sugar marketer, adding rivalry in marketing that mills controlled.
summary: A mandatory code governing supply contracts between sugar mills and cane growers, including growers' right to choose who markets their sugar. It brings competition into sugar marketing.

title: Port of Darwin 99-year lease (Northern Territory)
reasons: competition -1: Moves a port monopoly to a private owner under light-handed price regulation. | capital +1: A private owner with a long lease has incentives to invest, and the proceeds funded other infrastructure.
summary: A long-term lease of a state-owned port to a private operator. Private owners may invest and run the port more efficiently, but a port is a local monopoly and lease terms can raise charges or deter rival ports.

title: Port of Brisbane 99-year lease (Queensland)
reasons: competition -1: Moves a port monopoly to a private owner under light-handed price regulation. | capital +1: A private owner with a long lease has incentives to invest, and the proceeds funded other infrastructure.

title: Port of Melbourne 50-year lease (Victoria)
reasons: competition -1: Moves a port monopoly to a private owner under light-handed price regulation. | capital +1: A private owner with a long lease has incentives to invest, and the proceeds funded other infrastructure. | entry-exit -1: The lease obliges the state to compensate the lessee if a competing container port is built before 2066.
summary: A long-term lease of a state-owned port to a private operator. Private owners may invest and run the port more efficiently, but a port is a local monopoly and lease terms can raise charges or deter rival ports.

title: Safe harbour from insolvent trading for directors attempting a turnaround
reasons: entry-exit +1: Lowers the personal risk of trying to restructure a struggling firm, making exit and turnaround decisions better.
summary: Directors who pursue a reasonable turnaround plan are protected from personal liability for insolvent trading. It can save viable firms from premature liquidation, though evidence on how often it is used is limited.

title: Small business restructuring and simplified liquidation
reasons: entry-exit +1: Cheaper restructuring and liquidation for small firms lower the cost of exit. | burden +1: A simpler process cuts the administrative cost of insolvency for small businesses.
summary: Small incorporated businesses can use a cheaper debtor-in-possession restructuring and a simplified liquidation. Cheaper exit and restructuring speed the move of resources out of failing firms, though it may also keep weak firms going.

title: Insurance duty abolished (ACT)
reasons: prices-taxes +1: Removes a tax that discouraged insurance, replaced by a broad land tax.
summary: Abolished duty on insurance premiums, replacing the revenue with general rates. People and businesses pay less for cover, as the Henry Review recommended.

title: Duty on business insurance phased out (Victoria)
reasons: prices-taxes +1: Removes a tax that discouraged businesses from insuring, step by step to 2033.
summary: Phases out duty on business insurance over ten years. It lowers the cost of cover for businesses and removes a tax the Henry Review recommended abolishing; duty on household insurance remains.

title: Instant asset write-off threshold increases and temporary full expensing
reasons: capital +2: Immediate deduction lowers the after-tax cost of investing across most industries. | prices-taxes -1: Temporary, threshold-based concessions favour some assets and firm sizes and pull investment forward.
summary: Small and then most businesses could deduct the cost of new equipment immediately, with temporary full expensing from 2020 to 2023. It lowered the cost of capital across the economy, though some investment was brought forward rather than added, and the thresholds and time limits distort which assets and firms benefit.

title: Legal Profession Uniform Law (NSW)
reasons: market-integration +1: A common legal services market across participating states replaces separate regimes. | burden +1: Firms working in several participating states comply with one set of rules.
summary: One set of rules for lawyers across participating states, so firms can practise across borders under a single regime. A modest gain for a national legal services market.

title: Legal Profession Uniform Law (Victoria)
reasons: market-integration +1: A common legal services market across participating states replaces separate regimes. | burden +1: Firms working in several participating states comply with one set of rules.
summary: One set of rules for lawyers across participating states, so firms can practise across borders under a single regime. A modest gain for a national legal services market.

title: Western Australia joins the Legal Profession Uniform Law
reasons: market-integration +1: A common legal services market across participating states replaces separate regimes. | burden +1: Firms working in several participating states comply with one set of rules.
summary: One set of rules for lawyers across participating states, so firms can practise across borders under a single regime. A modest gain for a national legal services market.

title: Moratorium on new takeaway liquor licences (Northern Territory)
reasons: entry-exit -2: A moratorium on new takeaway licences blocks entry into liquor retailing.
summary: No new takeaway liquor licences for two years in the Northern Territory, to reduce alcohol harm. It blocks entry into liquor retailing and protects existing bottle shops.

title: Freeze on new late-night liquor licences lifted (Victoria)
reasons: entry-exit +2: Lifts a freeze on new late-night licences, allowing new venues.
summary: Ended a 15-year freeze on new liquor licences trading after 1am in four inner Melbourne areas, in favour of risk-based assessment.

title: Sydney CBD and Kings Cross lockout and last-drinks laws (NSW)
reasons: entry-exit -2: A freeze on new liquor licences in the precinct blocks new venues. | competition -1: Lockouts and earlier last drinks limit how late venues can trade and compete.
summary: 1.30am lockouts, 3am last drinks and a freeze on new liquor licences in Sydney's CBD and Kings Cross, aimed at alcohol-related violence. Venues closed and activity moved elsewhere; the freeze shielded existing licences from new rivals.

title: Lockout laws repealed in the Sydney CBD (NSW)
reasons: competition +1: Restores late-night trading hours, letting venues compete on hours again.
summary: Removed the 1.30am lockout in the Sydney CBD and extended last drinks, restoring late-night trading.

title: Lockout laws lifted in Kings Cross (NSW)
reasons: competition +1: Restores late-night trading hours, letting venues compete on hours again.
summary: Removed the 1.30am lockout in Kings Cross and extended last drinks, restoring late-night trading.

title: Tackling Alcohol-Fuelled Violence: 2am statewide trading cap (Queensland)
reasons: competition -1: Shorter permitted trading hours limit late-night venues' ability to compete on hours.
summary: Cut the latest liquor trading time to 2am statewide (3am in some precincts). Shorter hours limit how venues can compete and may push marginal venues out.

title: Mandatory and suspensory merger notification regime
reasons: competition +1: Mandatory review of acquisitions, including serial ones, should block more mergers that lessen competition.
summary: Acquisitions above set thresholds must be notified to the ACCC and wait for clearance, including serial acquisitions. It should stop more mergers that would lessen competition, such as roll-ups of local markets.

title: Revitalised National Competition Policy
reasons: market-integration +1: Aligning standards with international ones and national licensing for some occupations integrate markets. | entry-exit +1: Zoning and planning reform lowers barriers to new businesses and housing. | labour +1: Occupational licensing reform eases moves between states and occupations. | innovation +1: Right to repair and modern methods of construction ease adoption of better technology.
summary: Commonwealth, state and territory treasurers agreed a revitalised National Competition Policy, with payments for reforms to zoning, standards, occupational licensing, heavy vehicles and the right to repair. The Productivity Commission's modelling puts the gains from a wider package at 1.0 to 1.7% of GDP. Not yet in force.

title: National Energy Customer Framework adopted (ACT)
reasons: market-integration +1: One national retailer authorisation and common customer protections replace state regimes. | burden +1: Retailers operating in several states comply with one framework instead of several.
summary: Adopting the National Energy Retail Law replaced a state retailer licence with one national authorisation and common customer rules. It lowers the cost for a retailer of serving customers in several states.

reasons: burden -1: Adds design and compliance costs to every new home, which weigh most on small builders.
summary: Adopts the 2022 National Construction Code's higher energy efficiency (7-star) and livable housing standards for new homes. Both sets of provisions were adopted. The standards cut running costs and improve access, which are not weighed here; they also add to the cost of building.

title: Ban on non-compete, no-poach and wage-fixing clauses
reasons: labour +2: Removes a barrier to moving between jobs for a large share of the workforce. | entry-exit +1: Workers can leave to start competing firms.
summary: Would ban non-compete clauses for workers earning below a threshold, and no-poach and wage-fixing agreements, from 2027. About one in five workers has a non-compete; removing them lets workers move to rivals or start firms. Not yet legislated.

title: Pharmacists treat uncomplicated urinary tract infections (ACT)
reasons: labour +1: Widens pharmacists' scope of practice, using their training more fully and freeing GP time. | competition +1: Adds pharmacies as an alternative supplier of a service that needed a GP prescription.
summary: Trained community pharmacists can treat uncomplicated urinary tract infections, a service that needed a GP visit. It uses pharmacists' skills more fully and adds a convenient supplier; medical groups raise concerns about quality and antibiotic use.

title: 60-day dispensing of PBS medicines
reasons: prices-taxes +1: Halves the dispensing fees and co-payments paid per month of medicine, removing a cost that bought no extra service.
summary: Prescribers may order two months' supply of eligible medicines. Patients make fewer pharmacy visits and pay one co-payment for two months; pharmacies dispense less often.

title: Sunset on pharmacy location rules removed
reasons: entry-exit -2: Entrenches rules that bar new PBS-approved pharmacies near existing ones.
summary: Removed the sunset on the pharmacy location rules, so rules that stop a new PBS-approved pharmacy opening near existing ones continue indefinitely. The Harper Review recommended removing them as a barrier to entry that protects incumbents.

title: Pharmacy business licensing and ownership regime (Queensland)
reasons: entry-exit -1: A new pharmacy business licence and enforced ownership limits restrict who may open or buy a pharmacy. | burden -1: Owners must hold a licence and report material interests.
summary: A new licensing regime and council enforce Queensland's rules on who may own a pharmacy. It adds a licensing layer and tightens enforcement of ownership limits that keep out other business models.

title: Employment zones reform (New South Wales)
reasons: entry-exit +1: Wider permitted uses lower the planning barrier to opening new businesses. | burden +1: Fewer, simpler zones mean fewer rezoning and development applications.
summary: Replaced business and industrial zones with simpler employment zones that permit a wider range of uses. More places where new businesses, including supermarkets, can open without rezoning.

title: Transport Oriented Development program (New South Wales)
reasons: capital +1: Building as of right lowers the approval time and risk of housing investment. | labour +1: More homes near rail lines let more workers reach more jobs.
summary: Mid-rise housing is allowed near designated railway stations without rezoning. Lower approval risk and time for building homes where workers can reach more jobs.

title: Booked hire licences and booking entities (Queensland)
reasons: entry-exit +1: A booked hire licence gives new operators a permanent legal route into point-to-point transport. | innovation +1: Puts app-based booking on a settled legal footing.
summary: Licences for booked hire services and booking entities completed Queensland's legal framework for ride-share alongside capped taxi licences.

title: Metropolitan taxi licence cap removed, buyback and annual licences (South Australia)
reasons: entry-exit +2: Ends the cap on metropolitan taxi licences. | prices-taxes +1: Removes the per-trip passenger levy that added to fares.
summary: South Australia is buying back perpetual metropolitan taxi licences and replacing them with annual licences open to all accredited operators, and lifted the passenger levy.

title: R&D Tax Incentive replaces the R&D tax concession
reasons: innovation +1: A refundable offset lowers the cost of R&D for smaller and loss-making firms.
summary: The R&D Tax Incentive replaced the R&D concession, with a refundable offset for smaller companies, including those making losses. It lowers the cost of R&D for young and challenger firms.

title: R&D Tax Incentive redesign (premium rates, intensity tiers)
reasons: innovation +1: A more generous refundable offset lowers the cost of R&D for small firms.
summary: Redesigned the R&D Tax Incentive: a more generous refundable offset for companies under $20 million turnover, and offsets for larger companies that rise with R&D intensity.

title: Conveyance duty phased out in favour of general rates (ACT)
reasons: prices-taxes +2: Replaces a highly distorting transaction tax with a broad annual land tax. | labour +1: Lowers the cost of moving home, including to take a better job.
summary: Swaps stamp duty for an annual land tax, step by step over 20 years. One of the most efficient tax reforms in Australia: it lowers the cost of moving home and lets property change hands more easily.

title: Retail electricity price deregulation (NSW)
reasons: prices-taxes +1: Retail prices follow costs rather than a regulated tariff. | competition +1: Retailers are free to compete on price and offers; the gain is smaller for customers who do not shop around.
summary: Removed regulated retail electricity prices once regulators judged competition effective. Prices can follow costs and retailers compete freely, though many customers who never switched stayed on high standing offers.

reasons: prices-taxes +1: Retail prices follow costs rather than a regulated tariff. | competition +1: Retailers are free to compete on price and offers; the gain is smaller for customers who do not shop around.

title: Statewide Boxing Day trading (NSW)
reasons: competition +1: Longer permitted hours let retailers compete on convenience and give shoppers more choice.
summary: Allowed shops across New South Wales to open on Boxing Day. One extra trading day a year: a small gain. The Productivity Commission has recommended removing trading hours restrictions altogether.

title: Standardised and extended trading hours (Queensland)
reasons: competition +1: Longer permitted hours let retailers compete on convenience. | burden +1: Simple statutory hours replace a complex set of trading hours orders.
summary: Replaced Queensland's trading hours orders with statutory hours: in south-east Queensland, shops may open 7am to 9pm Monday to Saturday and on Sundays. Longer, simpler hours let shops compete on convenience.

title: Adelaide CBD tourist precinct trading hours (SA)
reasons: competition +1: Longer permitted hours let retailers compete on convenience and give shoppers more choice.
summary: Extended shop trading hours in the Adelaide CBD only, as a tourist precinct. The gain is confined to one area and may shift sales from suburban shops. The Productivity Commission has recommended removing trading hours restrictions altogether.

title: Extended Sunday and Boxing Day trading (SA)
reasons: competition +1: Longer permitted hours let retailers compete on convenience and give shoppers more choice.
summary: Allowed Adelaide shops to open from 9am on Sundays and suburban shops on Boxing Day. The Productivity Commission has recommended removing trading hours restrictions altogether.

title: Sunday trading in metropolitan Perth (WA)
reasons: competition +1: Longer permitted hours let retailers compete on convenience and give shoppers more choice.
summary: Allowed general shops in metropolitan Perth to open on Sundays and most public holidays. The Productivity Commission has recommended removing trading hours restrictions altogether.

reasons: entry-exit -1: A 180-night cap on unhosted stays in Greater Sydney limits supply from hosts. | burden -1: Hosts must register and meet fire safety and code requirements.
summary: A code of conduct, a mandatory register, fire safety rules and a 180-night cap on unhosted stays in Greater Sydney. It limits short-term rental supply and protects hotels from some competition; effects on long-term rental supply are not weighed here.

title: Short stay levy of 7.5% (Victoria)
reasons: prices-taxes -1: A levy on one type of accommodation but not its rivals distorts guests' choices.
summary: A 7.5% levy on short stays booked in residential premises, from which hotels, motels and caravan parks are exempt. It tilts competition towards incumbent commercial accommodation; its aim, more homes for long-term rental, is not weighed here.

title: Mandatory short-term rental accommodation register (WA)
reasons: burden -1: Hosts must register and show registration numbers on every listing. | entry-exit -1: Phased-in planning approvals add a condition for new unhosted short-term rentals.
summary: A mandatory statewide register for short-term rentals, with planning approvals phased in. It adds costs and conditions for hosts; effects on long-term rental supply are not weighed here.

title: Small bar licence (New South Wales)
reasons: entry-exit +1: Lower fees and simpler requirements let small operators open venues a full hotel licence would deter.
summary: A cheaper, simpler licence class for small venues, separate from hotel licences. It lowers the cost of opening a small bar.

title: Small bar licence (Western Australia)
reasons: entry-exit +1: Lower fees and simpler requirements let small operators open venues a full hotel licence would deter.
summary: A cheaper, simpler licence class for small venues, separate from hotel licences. It lowers the cost of opening a small bar.

title: Lower company tax rate for base rate entities, with a rising turnover threshold
reasons: capital +1: A lower tax rate raises after-tax returns on investment for smaller companies. | entry-exit -1: The five-point jump in the tax rate at the threshold discourages firms from growing past it.
summary: A lower company tax rate (now 25%) for companies under a turnover threshold that rose to $50 million. It raises after-tax returns for smaller firms, but the gap between the two rates is a tax on growing past the threshold.

title: Unfair contract terms made illegal with penalties; broader small business coverage
reasons: competition +1: Penalties deter larger firms from imposing one-sided terms on consumers and small businesses.
summary: Using unfair terms in standard form contracts now attracts civil penalties, and more small businesses are covered. Stronger deterrence of one-sided terms; firms bear a one-off cost of reviewing their contracts.

title: Unfair contract terms protection extended to small business
reasons: competition +1: Limits larger firms' ability to impose one-sided terms on small businesses.
summary: Unfair terms in standard form contracts with small businesses became void. It curbs one-sided terms that larger firms impose on small suppliers, franchisees and customers.

reasons: entry-exit +1: Opens state training subsidies to private providers, adding suppliers. | labour +1: Subsidised places with student choice of provider widen access to training.
summary: Training subsidies follow the student to any approved public or private provider. More providers and places can lift skills, but quality and cost control have been problems, most of all in Victoria and South Australia.

reasons: market-integration -2: Restricts foreign vessels to voyage-limited temporary licences, closing much of coastal freight to the cheapest ships. | burden -1: Temporary licence applications, notices and variations add delay and cost for shippers.

title: Environment protection law reform (EPBC) and National EPA
reasons: capital +1: Faster, more certain approvals lower the cost of delay for new projects. | burden -1: Stricter national environmental standards add compliance requirements.
summary: Reforms to national environment law and a new National EPA promise faster, more certain approvals alongside stricter national standards. The productivity effect depends on standards and processes still being made.

title: Major Bank Levy
reasons: prices-taxes -1: A tax on some banks' liabilities distorts funding costs and can be passed on to all borrowers. | competition +1: Narrows the major banks' funding cost advantage over smaller rivals.
summary: A levy of 0.06% a year on the liabilities of the five largest banks. It narrows their funding cost advantage over smaller banks, but as a tax on one set of firms' funding it can be passed on to borrowers.

title: Motor vehicle service and repair information sharing scheme
reasons: competition +1: Lets independent repairers compete with dealers for servicing and repairs. | innovation +1: Access to repair data and tools spreads the ability to service new vehicle technology.
summary: Car makers must give independent repairers the same service and repair information as dealers. Independents can compete with dealer networks: a right-to-repair reform.

title: Petroleum Retail Marketing Sites and Franchise Acts repealed; Oilcode introduced
reasons: entry-exit +1: Removes limits on how many sites refiners could operate directly.
summary: Repealed limits on oil refiners running service stations directly, and introduced a mandatory Oilcode for fuel reselling. Refiners can integrate into retail, which may lower costs or squeeze independents.

title: Your Future, Your Super annual performance test
reasons: competition +1: Naming and barring underperformers pushes members to better funds. | entry-exit +1: Repeated failure forces poor products to close or merge. | innovation -1: Funds are judged against set benchmarks, which discourages investing differently from them.
summary: MySuper products that fail an annual performance test must tell members, and products that fail twice may not take new members. It pushes members and assets to better funds, though benchmark-based tests encourage funds to stay close to the benchmark.

title: Sydney Airport slot management reform
reasons: entry-exit +1: Stricter use-it-or-lose-it rules free slots for new and smaller airlines.
summary: Tighter slot rules at Sydney Airport, to stop incumbents holding slots they do not use and to give new entrants access. Slot access is the main barrier to new airlines on Sydney routes; the curfew and movement cap remain.

title: Vapes restricted to pharmacy supply
reasons: entry-exit -2: Restricts lawful supply to pharmacies, closing the market to other retailers.
summary: Vapes may be sold only by pharmacies for therapeutic use, after bans on imports of disposable and non-therapeutic vapes. It closes other legal retail channels and may push supply to illicit sellers.

title: Wheat export single desk abolished
reasons: entry-exit +2: Removes a statutory export monopoly, letting accredited exporters enter.
summary: Ended AWB's statutory single desk for bulk wheat exports: accredited exporters compete to buy growers' grain.

title: Minimum floor price for alcohol (Northern Territory)
reasons: prices-taxes -1: A price floor holds the cheapest drinks above what they cost to supply. | competition -1: Retailers cannot compete on price below the floor.
summary: Liquor may not be sold in the Northern Territory below $1.30 a standard drink. A legal price floor, aimed at alcohol harm, stops retailers competing on price below it.

title: As-of-right taxi licences at a set annual fee (Victoria)
reasons: entry-exit +2: Ends the numerical cap on taxi licences.
summary: New taxi licences became available at any time to approved applicants for a set annual fee, ending the cap on licence numbers in Melbourne and urban zones.

title: Queensland stays out of automatic mutual recognition
reasons: labour -1: Keeps the application and fee licensed workers face when moving between Queensland and other states. | market-integration -1: Keeps Queensland's licensed services market separate from the scheme the other states share.
summary: Queensland stays out of automatic mutual recognition, so licensed workers moving into or out of the state still apply and pay for a separate registration.

title: Planning and zoning restrictions (ACT)
reasons: prices-taxes -2: Zoning keeps house prices well above the cost of supply: a large distortion in the largest asset market. | entry-exit -1: Zoning and approvals limit the sites open to new businesses; the Harper Review found planning rules can favour incumbents. | burden -1: Development approvals add paperwork, holding costs and delay to building homes and business premises.

title: Stamp duty on residential property transfers (New South Wales)
reasons: prices-taxes -2: A transaction tax in the largest asset market, with an efficiency cost Treasury puts at 72 cents per extra dollar raised. | labour -1: Raises the cost of moving home, so fewer people move to take better jobs.
summary: A tax on buying a home, paid every time property changes hands. It discourages people from moving, including for work, and is one of the least efficient taxes in Australia; a broad annual land tax raising the same revenue would cost far less.

title: Anti-dumping and countervailing duties
reasons: market-integration -1: Extra duties shelter some domestic producers from import competition and raise costs for downstream users.
summary: Extra duties on imports found to be dumped or subsidised. They help a few import-competing producers at a greater cost to users of those products; the Productivity Commission judged the net cost to be very small.

title: Australia Post's reserved letter service
reasons: entry-exit -2: Rivals are barred by law from carrying ordinary letters: an exclusive right.
summary: A legal monopoly on carrying ordinary letters. It shuts out rivals in a market that is now small and shrinking, so its cost to productivity is limited.

title: Mandatory standards that differ from international ones
reasons: market-integration -1: Bespoke and inconsistently incorporated standards make imported products and interstate suppliers meet different rules. | burden -1: Firms must buy and follow paywalled, sometimes outdated standards to comply with the law.
summary: Most standards that laws make mandatory are Australian-only, and states incorporate them inconsistently. Suppliers must meet rules the rest of the world does not use, which keeps out imports and adds cost; the Productivity Commission puts the gain from alignment at $1.1 to 3 billion a year.

title: Parallel import restrictions on books
reasons: market-integration -1: Restricts imports of books published overseas, sheltering local editions from price competition.
summary: Local publishers can block cheaper imported editions of books. It protects local publishing at the cost of higher prices for readers; the Productivity Commission has twice recommended repeal.

title: Foreign investment screening
reasons: market-integration -1: Screening, fees and conditions restrict foreign investment; the OECD's restrictiveness index for Australia rose in 2025. | capital -1: Approval times and the risk of conditions raise the cost of investing for foreign buyers.
summary: Approval, fees and conditions for foreign investment above set thresholds. They protect national security and other interests, which are not weighed here, but raise the cost and uncertainty of investment that brings capital, technology and competition.

title: The four pillars policy on bank mergers
reasons: competition -1: Shields the major banks from takeover by each other and locks in a four-bank structure (Productivity Commission, 2018).
summary: A ban on mergers among the four major banks. Competition law and the Treasurer's approval powers already allow such a merger to be blocked; the Productivity Commission found the policy protects a fixed market structure and removes the takeover threat that would otherwise discipline the majors.

title: Remaining import tariffs
reasons: market-integration -1: Tariffs shelter domestic producers from import competition and raise input costs. | burden -1: Importers must classify goods and prove origin to pay or avoid duty.
summary: The tariffs left after decades of reform, mostly 5%. They raise prices for buyers of imported goods and inputs and add customs paperwork, for little protection.

title: Sydney Airport curfew and movement cap
reasons: entry-exit -1: Scarce peak slots, kept by the airlines that use them, make entry to Sydney routes harder.
summary: The curfew and the hourly cap limit how many flights can use Sydney Airport, so peak slots are scarce and mostly held by incumbents. New airlines struggle to get them.

title: Domestic gas reservation (Western Australia)
reasons: prices-taxes -1: Holds domestic gas prices below their export value, so gas does not go to its most valued use. | market-integration -1: Diverts gas from export markets by condition of approval.
summary: Reserves part of WA's gas for local users. It holds domestic gas prices below export prices, which favours gas-using industries over others and weakens the incentive to develop new supply; the Productivity Commission found such policies cost more than they deliver.
